pac_metadata.title: Edo Period Japan (17th Century)
pac_metadata.description: The 17th century marked the beginning of the Edo Period under the Tokugawa Shogunate, establishing over 250 years of peace and stability. This era saw the consolidation of central power, the implementation of a strict social hierarchy, and the initial stages of the sakoku isolationist policy. It was a time of cultural flourishing and urban growth centered around the new capital, Edo.

dwellings.description: Common homes for different classes, primarily made of wood and paper.

public_structures.description: Buildings for government, commerce, and public gathering.
key_features: Ichiba (markets) - often open-air or simple stalls
Intricate wooden carvings and painted details

construction_techniques_materials.description: Predominantly wood-based, utilizing joinery and modular design.

everyday_clothing_male.description: Standard garments worn by men across various classes.
items: Hakama (divided or undivided skirt-trousers, less common for merchants/farmers)

ceremonial_clothing_male.description: Formal attire for samurai and officials.
items: Kamishimo (set of kataginu jacket and hakama trousers)
Kosode (worn in layers or as outer garment)

ceremonial_clothing_female.description: More elaborate layered kosode and formal obi styles.
items: Uchikake (formal outer robe, often heavily decorated)

materials_colors_decorative_elements.description: Fabrics, dyes, and patterns used in clothing.

status_indicators.description: Elements of clothing that indicated social standing.
key_indicators: Quality and material of fabric (silk vs. cotton/hemp)
Specific colors or patterns restricted to certain classes (e.g., purple)
Length of sleeves (especially for women - longer for younger/unmarried)

weapons_armor.description: Weapons primarily associated with the samurai class, and the evolving nature of armor.
key_features: Katana (long sword) and Wakizashi (short sword) - daishō set for samurai
Armor (gusoku) - evolving towards less practical, more decorative forms by late 17th century

tools.description: Common tools used in daily life, agriculture, and crafts.
key_features: Cooking utensils (iron pots, ceramic bowls, wooden chopsticks)
Norimono (more elaborate palanquins for high status)
Horses (primarily for samurai and official messengers)
Wooden boats (for river and coastal travel)

characteristics: Often focused on courtly life and literature

key_motifs: Pine, Bamboo, Plum (Three Friends of Winter - resilience)
Tigers (strength, protection - often paired with bamboo)

materials_methods.description: Mediums and techniques used in artistic creation.
key_elements: Sumi ink on paper or silk
Mineral and plant pigments (gofun - shell white, malachite green, azurite blue)

key_imagery: Scenes from The Tale of Genji or Tale of Heike
Images of deities and Buddhist figures
Depictions of famous battles or historical events
Portraits of famous poets, scholars, or historical figures
Scenes of daily life, festivals, and city views (increasingly with Ukiyo-e)

natural_colors.description: Colors derived from natural materials and un-dyed fibers.
key_colors: Earth tones (browns, greys, ochres from mud, wood, stone)
Natural whites (from unbleached cotton/hemp, paper, plaster)
Greens (from foliage and natural aging of materials)

dyes_pigments.description: Common sources for colored dyes and pigments.
key_sources: Mineral pigments (green from malachite, blue from azurite, red from cinnabar, white from shell)

status_associations.description: Colors that indicated social status or had symbolic meaning.
key_associations: Purple (Murasaki) - often restricted to high ranks, associated with elegance/nobility
Specific shades/combinations - could indicate rank, profession, or occasion
Vibrancy and richness of color - often correlated with wealth and status
Muted or simple colors - common for farmers and lower classes

classes: Outcasts (eta, hinin - below the main classes)
social_structure.leadership: The Shogun held ultimate political power, supported by the Bakufu (military government). The Emperor was a symbolic figurehead in Kyoto. Daimyo (feudal lords) governed domains under the Shogun's authority. Village and town affairs were managed by local officials and councils.

daily_life.typical_routines: Varied by class. Farmers worked the fields from dawn to dusk. Samurai attended to administrative duties, trained, or served their lords. Artisans and merchants worked in shops and homes. Life often revolved around the agricultural cycle, work obligations, and family duties.
daily_life.food: Primarily rice, vegetables (daikon, eggplant, greens), beans, tofu, fish, seaweed, pickles, miso, soy sauce, tea. Meat consumption was rare for religious reasons. Meals were typically simple and based on seasonal availability.
daily_life.occupations: Farming (over 80% of population), samurai (warriors, officials), artisans (potters, weavers, carpenters, swordsmiths, etc.), merchants (shopkeepers, traders, moneylenders), fishermen, laborers, entertainers.
daily_life.family_life: Patriarchal structure with the male head of household (koshu) having authority. Emphasis on the 'ie' (household/family lineage) over individuals. Arranged marriages were common. Children were raised to understand their social role and duties; discipline and obedience were valued.

rituals.religious_practices: Buddhism (various schools, strongly associated with death rites and family lineage) and Shinto (indigenous practices focused on purity, nature worship, and local deities). Confucianism influenced social ethics and governance. Syncretism was common.

life_cycle.birth: Involved Shinto purification rituals, presenting the child to the local kami at a shrine (e.g., Omiyamairi).
life_cycle.coming_of_age: Genpuku (for boys, around 15, signifying adulthood and eligibility for marriage/service) and Mogi (for girls, around 12-16, marking eligibility for marriage).
life_cycle.marriage: Predominantly arranged marriages for the benefit of the 'ie'. Ceremonies involved formal introductions, exchange of gifts, and a ritual sake exchange (san-san-kudo).
life_cycle.death: Buddhist funeral rites were standard, followed by elaborate mourning periods and ancestor veneration at the family Buddhist temple and home altar (Butsudan).

rituals.seasonal_celebrations: Numerous Matsuri (festivals) tied to Shinto shrines (harvest, purification, local deities). Significant holidays included New Year (Oshogatsu - family gatherings, shrine visits), Obon (honoring ancestors), Tanabata (star festival).
rituals.important_ceremonies: Tea Ceremony (Chanoyu), formalized visits between samurai and officials, ceremonies at shrines and temples, poetry gatherings.

entertainment.games: Go, Shogi (Japanese chess), Sugoroku (board game), Karuta (card games), dice games, various children's games, martial arts practice (for samurai).
entertainment.music: Shamisen, Koto, Shakuhachi, Taiko drums. Music was part of theatre (Noh, later Kabuki), religious rituals, festivals, and private entertainment.
entertainment.storytelling_traditions: Rakugo (comic solo storytelling), Kōdan (historical/military tales), various forms of folk tales and legends, Noh and Kabuki theatre.
entertainment.other_leisure_activities: Attending Noh and later Kabuki theatre, visiting pleasure quarters (Yoshiwara in Edo), poetry composition (Haiku, Waka), flower viewing (Hanami), moon viewing (Tsukimi), visiting hot springs, wrestling (Sumo).

taboos_and_codes.behavioral_expectations: Emphasis on politeness, respect for hierarchy, fulfilling duty (giri), maintaining social harmony (wa), indirect communication, controlled emotional expression, loyalty to one's lord and family.
taboos_and_codes.taboos_and_forbidden_activities: Open defiance of authority, public displays of intense emotion, bringing shame upon one's family or lord, disrespecting elders, certain types of contact with outcasts, unauthorized travel or changing social status (especially for lower classes).
taboos_and_codes.honor_and_shame_concepts: Central to identity, especially for samurai. Honor was tied to loyalty, duty, courage, lineage, and status. Shame resulted from failure, cowardice, disloyalty, or misconduct. Seppuku (ritual suicide) was a samurai method to restore honor.
taboos_and_codes.hospitality_customs: Formalized. Guests were received with politeness, offered tea and refreshments. The host was expected to make the guest feel welcome and comfortable within established social norms. Hospitality was also a duty between family members and within communities.

farewells.meaning: Go and come back safely (response to Ittekimasu)

common_expressions.meaning: Excuse me / Sorry / Thank you (depending on context)

formal_speech_elements: Keigo (honorific language) including specific verb conjugations (-masu, -gozaimasu)
Humble forms for actions by the speaker

oaths.meaning: I swear by the kami (Shinto gods)
To swear by writing one's name in blood (on a document)

patterns: Surname + Given name (primarily for Samurai and higher classes)
Childhood names (yōmyō) before coming of age
Buddhist names upon retirement or death
Women often had names ending in -ko, -hime (princess), -gozen
common_elements: Samurai names often used characters passed down or granted by a lord
Common names often reflected virtues, nature, or auspicious meanings

patterns: Descriptive names based on geography (e.g., rivers, mountains, valleys)
Names referencing local features (gates, bridges, temples, shrines)
Names based on historical events or local legends

title_systems: Official titles: Shogun, Daimyo, Hatamoto, Gokenin, various court ranks
Occupational titles: Samurai, Bonze (priest), Buyo (merchant), Hyakusho (farmer), various artisan titles
Honorifics used in address: -sama, -dono, -shi, -san (becoming more common), -kun
Family/Relationship terms used for address (e.g., Otō-san - father)

name_meanings.common_elements: Names often convey auspicious meanings like longevity, strength, wisdom, or reference nature.
name_meanings.meaning: Reflecting hopes for the person, virtues, or natural beauty. Samurai names could reflect loyalty or receive characters from lords.
Typically descriptive of the location's physical features, history, or local landmarks.

language_structure.formal_vs_informal: Japanese heavily utilized 'Keigo' (honorific language) to distinguish formal speech used towards superiors or strangers from informal speech (tameguchi) used among equals, family, and close friends.
language_structure.status_indicators: Social status, age, and relationship determined the level of politeness (Keigo) used. Choice of vocabulary, verb conjugations, and honorifics explicitly marked the speaker's relationship to the listener and anyone being discussed.
language_structure.poetic_specialized: Poetic forms like Haiku (5-7-5 syllables) and Waka (5-7-5-7-7 syllables) were prominent. Formal writing and literature used classical Japanese grammar (bungo), distinct from the spoken language. Jargons existed for various professions and social groups.
common_metaphors: Metaphors drawn from nature (seasons, animals, plants)
Expressions related to Buddhist or Shinto concepts
Proverbs (kotowaza) reflecting traditional wisdom and daily life

scripts: Texts often mixed Kanji and Hiragana, sometimes using Katakana for emphasis or foreign words.
inscriptions_texts: Woodblock prints (ukiyo-e) often included captions or dialogue
materials_methods: Washi (Japanese paper) made from plant fibers
Woodblock printing (mokuhan) for books, prints, and documents
Writing often done on scrolls (makimono, kakemono) or folded books
Carved wood or stone for durable inscriptions
writing_system.literacy: Literacy varied significantly by class and region. Samurai and clergy were generally literate. Merchants often had functional literacy for business. Literacy was lower among farmers but varied depending on local conditions and status. Women's literacy varied by class, with some samurai women and women in urban merchant families receiving education.

geography.settlements: Settlements were diverse: large cities (Edo, Kyoto, Osaka), castle towns, shukuba (post towns) along highways, farming villages in plains and valleys, and fishing villages along the coast. Often located near water sources and defensible positions.
natural_resources: Minerals (copper, silver, gold in limited quantities)

climate.seasonal_variations: Distinct four seasons: hot, humid summers; cold winters with snow (especially in the north and mountains); pleasant spring and autumn; a pronounced rainy season (tsuyu) in early summer.
typical_weather_conditions: Clear days in spring and autumn
climate.climate_challenges_and_adaptations: Challenges included typhoons (requiring sturdy structures), heavy rain (leading to elevated floors, permeable walls, drainage), and summer heat/humidity (requiring ventilation and open structures). Adaptations included specific architecture (e.g., minka, castle design), seasonal clothing, and reliance on natural ventilation.
climate.weather_related_beliefs: Kami (deities) were associated with weather phenomena (e.g., thunder, wind, rain), influencing prayers for good harvests, protection from storms, and rituals to appease weather deities.

lighting_conditions.daylight_patterns: Daylight patterns followed standard temperate zone variations, dictating the primary rhythm of daily life. Activity typically began at sunrise and ended near sunset, especially outside major urban centers.
artificial_lighting_methods: Oil lamps (using oils like rapeseed or fish oil)
Candles (wax from sumac trees or beeswax - more expensive)
Paper lanterns (andon for indoor standing, chochin for portable/hanging)
lighting_conditions.light_related_cultural_practices: Daily life structured around daylight; evening activities and travel were limited without artificial light. Lanterns were significant in festivals and ceremonies. Paper screens (shoji) provided soft, diffuse interior light during the day.
lighting_conditions.visual_atmosphere: Interiors often featured soft, filtered light through paper screens. Exteriors varied from brightly lit fields/coasts during the day to deep darkness at night outside major cities. Urban centers had pockets of light from lamps and lanterns after dark.

human_activity_sounds: Sounds from markets, ports, and workshops
music_and_ceremonial_sounds: Temple and shrine bells and drums
Sounds from Noh and Kabuki theater
soundscape.silence_and_noise_patterns: Relatively quiet in rural areas and at night, especially away from settlements. Noisy in cities, markets, ports, and during festivals. Temples and shrines could offer pockets of relative silence, contrasting with surrounding activity.
